rationale: A wins because it knows where the floorboards are weak and refuses to step through them. Its refused angle, "Canva's recent AI acquisition is already powering its enterprise suite," correctly kills the speculative acquisition link; B keeps that same bad move alive as "Canva bought an AI image startup, then shipped it as a brand-safety feature." B is sharper in places, especially "24,000 paid teams, 220 million users — and Canva can't name one enterprise customer," but one confidently invented kept angle is how founders end up pitching fiction with a logo on it.
gaps_in_A: "220 million free users" overstates the fact pattern. The update says 220 million monthly users, not that they are all free users.

"Profitable, private, and valued at $26B: Canva goes hunting for enterprise revenue" is plausible but a little too motive-heavy; the update does not say enterprise revenue is the strategic reason for the launch.
The AI-governance angle is good, but "Enterprises don't want raw generative AI" needs at least one buyer or market proof point before it can carry as a trend, not just a Canva example.
The Adobe/Microsoft counterposition needs more product-level specificity on what Canva would actually displace; A flags this, but the angle still leans on broad incumbent conflict.
gaps_in_B: "Canva bought an AI image startup, then shipped it as a brand-safety feature" invents the causal link the update does not provide. This is the big sin.
"The acquisition and the AI generation feature land together" is not in the facts. "Recently acquired" plus "launched AI tool" does not equal same product line.
"the admin layer ... is the exact moat Adobe has used" may be true, but it is outside the supplied update and presented as fact rather than a proof need.
"Next step: newsjack-detector" is the wrong next move for this asset. The immediate blocker is proof: named customer, enterprise split, acquisition linkage, then journalist-fit-check.
